newsitem.title: CHINA: INTERVIEW-China foreign debt may rise - bank chief.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-China foreign debt may rise - bank chief.

text.p: China's foreign debt reached $109.5 billion at the end of June and had been expanding by about $10 billion a year over the last five years, central bank governor Dai Xianglong said.
The governor of the People's Bank of China said that the nation's foreign exchange reserves, about $96 billion at the end of September, were at a comfortable level but hardly excessive.
"It is hard to say exactly where the debt level will be next year, but every year an additional $10 billion is possible," he told Reuters in an interview on Tuesday.
He said $10 billion had been the average annual addition to the debt level during China's eighth five-year plan from 1991 to 1995.
Asked whether the level of reserves was considered excessive, he said: "For a country of China's size, (the level of foreign exchange reserves) is not a big sum. We can only say it is comfortable."
Most of the reserves -- about 70 percent -- were held in dollars, he said.
Dai said that most of Beijing's debt was long-term but China needed reserves sufficient to maintain repayments as well as to be able to finance four months worth of imports.
It also had new needs for foreign currency following the recent move to make the renminbi -- China's currency -- convertible on the current account.
He described China's repayment status as good, although he conceded there were repayment problems with enterprises under the direction of local governments.
"We are very prudent in our borrowing," he said, adding that the debt service ratio was well within international warning levels.
"On the whole the repayment situation is good," Dai said.
"There are some local government-run enterprises that are overdue," he said.
"In the future the central bank and central government will strengthen (debt) management. If debts can't be repaid, then the guarantor must step in and repay."
But Dai also said foreign banks had a responsibility to ensure that credit went to deserving enterprises.
"Foreign creditors of Chinese enterprises must be selective in their lending," he said.
